information_integrity_failures.what: Managers disagreed about the direction of the FOMC probability, not merely its size.
information_integrity_failures.detail: Roughly half the field reported ~90% odds of a 25bp HIKE; the other half reported ~90% odds of a HOLD, several citing the same Investing.com Fed Rate Monitor. The session's WebSearch quota was exhausted early, so most managers fell back to WebFetch against whatever pages were reachable, and CME FedWatch, Reuters, CNBC and MarketWatch were all blocked or erroring. The books are therefore positioned on materially contradictory readings of the same event. This is a data-access artefact of the desk's environment, not a difference of judgment between managers, and it is recorded because it is invisible in the books themselves.

information_integrity_failures.what: At least three managers read other managers' in-flight decision files.
information_integrity_failures.detail: All 75 returns were written into one shared directory that every manager could read. Sonnet+tools price momentum states it cited 'parallel desk decision files already sitting in this poll's decisions folder'; Sonnet macro/sector rotation says its FOMC reading was 'confirmed independently against a sibling desk book's pull of the same data'; Sonnet price momentum says it 'cross-checked against a sibling desk book's independent research'. These managers' decisions are therefore not independent draws. The fault is the desk's — a shared readable directory — not the managers'. From week 10 each manager writes to its own directory and is told of no other.

information_integrity_failures.what: The desk told the last wave of managers about the disagreement; earlier waves were not told.
information_integrity_failures.detail: Waves 1-4 were polled without comment. Wave 5 was told that 'other desks are reading the rate-futures odds in opposite directions' and asked to name their source. That is desk-supplied information no manager could have obtained alone, and it was given to 7 of 47 managers. It was intended to improve sourcing discipline and it did, but it makes wave 5 non-comparable to the rest on this decision.

My strategy of record was written for a 'no-rate-cut macro'. That is no longer the regime and I was wrong to keep sizing for it. As of the 2026-09-15 tape the 10-year Treasury is at 5.01%, its highest since 2007; futures price a 92.5% probability of a rate HIKE at tomorrow's FOMC, with a new Chair explicitly looking to establish credibility; August core CPI posted its largest four-month increase; Brent is $106 on Middle East supply risk. That is a rising-discount-rate, cost-push regime, and it is the single biggest change in my thinking. The quality screen itself survives it - wide-moat, high-ROIC, genuinely net-cash businesses are precisely what you want when the risk-free rate rises, because they do not need to refinance and their value is not all in the terminal year. What does not survive it is WHICH quality names I owned. Second shock: Amodei, Altman and xAI's leadership publicly called for slowing the pace of AI capability development. Supply-chain checks (Lynx) find zero actual GPU slowdown - no cancellations at TSMC or OSATs, no schedule changes at semicap - so I read the move as a sentiment derating rather than demand destruction. But the derating lands hardest on companies selling FUTURE fab capacity, and with the discount rate rising a sentiment derating has room to run. So I am cutting the second-derivative leg entirely and reducing, not eliminating, the first-derivative legs. Three specific changes. (1) AMAT exits at 0% from 14%. Its business is fine - record $9.12bn quarter, +25%, positive Q4 guide - but it is down 27.6% over 63 days and 16.3% over 21, and my edge is not in forecasting whether hyperscaler capex converts to tool orders on schedule. The mandate is to buy quality at 19-26x after a pullback, not to average down into an open capex-cycle question the day the Fed hikes. (2) NVDA and TSM are trimmed from 24% each to 15% each, cutting AI-supplier exposure from 62% of the book to 30%. (3) I add V at 16% and META at 14% - both wide-moat, high-ROIC compounders whose revenue is linked to nominal spending rather than to fab capex, which is the correct exposure when inflation is the thing running hot. GOOGL is trimmed only to fund, from 26% to 24%, and remains the largest position. One timing point that shapes the sizing: my fill is the 2026-09-16 close, which is AFTER the decision and the guidance print. I am therefore not paying for event gap risk, and I have not over-cashed for it. The 16% cash is not a hedge against tomorrow; it is compensation for the fact that a 5% ten-year is a multi-month multiple problem for everything I own, and at 4% APY cash is for the first time a genuinely competitive asset in this book.
